newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Country profile of the mountain kingdom of Lesotho.
newsitem.headline: Country profile of the mountain kingdom of Lesotho.

text.p: Here are key facts about Lesotho, a southern African mountain kingdom surrounded by and reliant on regional economic giant South Africa.
Population: Nearly two million. Just over half the population is Roman Catholic, with most of the remainder following other Christian churches. Official languages are English and Sesotho.
Area: 30,355 sq km (11,720 sq miles). Lesotho is mountainous and landlocked.
Capital: Maseru.
Armed Forces: A small paramilitary unit has been transformed into a standing army, the Royal Lesotho Defence Force. There are around 2,000 police officers.
Economy: Most of Lesotho's trade is with South Africa and it belongs to a customs union with South Africa, Botswana and Swaziland.
The country is heavily dependent on remittances from miners working in South Africa. Customs receipts make up about half of government revenue.
A major scheme to dam mountain rivers and sell water to South Africa is under way.
Modern History: In the 19th century the Basotho resisted conquest by Afrikaner and British forces. After almost a century as a British protectorate Lesotho became independent in 1966.
Autocratic Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan declared null and void the results of the first general election in 1970 when it appeared his ruling Basotholand National Party would lose.
Jonathan was toppled by a bloodless military coup in January 1986 prompted by a land blockade by South Africa.

He was replaced by a Military Council headed by Major-General Justin Lekhanya which restored close relations with South Africa and shared power with King Moshoeshoe II, who had been reduced to a figurehead role under Jonathan's rule.

But after a power struggle with Lekhanya, Moshoeshoe fled into exile in London in 1990. In November the same year, the military ruler deposed him and replaced him with the king's British-educated son, Letsie III, in a non-executive capacity.
Lekhanya was himself ousted in a coup on April 30, 1991, and his place taken as head of the military government by Major-General Elias Ramaema.

Lesotho returned to civilian rule in March 1993 when Ntsu Mokhehle, a former guerrilla leader who fought against Jonathan, led his Basutoland Congress Party to victory in the country's first democratic elections in more than two decades.
In 1994 the country was hit by crises, including army mutinies and strikes by police and prison warders.
In April 1994 rebel soldiers shot dead Lesotho's deputy prime minister and detained four other ministers. Subsequently another minister was held at gunpoint.

King Letsie dissolved the government and parliament a month after the opposition Basutoland National Party asked him to stand down in favour of his father Moshoeshoe, dismiss Mokhehle's administration and form a national unity government.
After a period of uncertainty and implied threats of military action by regional states to restore the democratically-elected government, Letsie gave way.
The Mokhele government was reinstated in September 1994 and Moshoeshoe returned to the throne in January 1995.
He weathered a series of crises including strikes before dying in a car accident on January 15, 1996.
His son, King Letsie, was sworn in as his successor on February 7, 1996, at the age of 32.
